content: Vesicoureteric reflux (VUR) is a condition where urine flows backward from the bladder into the ureters. This retrograde flow of urine is associated with an increased risk of urinary tract infections (UTIs), which can lead to permanent renal parenchymal damage in children. Management strategies for VUR have traditionally focused on preventing UTIs through either long-term antibiotic prophylaxis or surgical correction of the reflux. This review aimed to assess the benefits and harms of various treatment options for primary VUR, including operative, non-operative, and no intervention approaches. The evidence was gathered from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and analyzed using rigorous statistical methods. A total of 34 studies involving 4001 children were included in the review. The interventions studied included long-term low-dose antibiotics, surgical reimplantation of the ureters, endoscopic injection treatments, probiotics, cranberry products, circumcision, and the use of oxybutynin. These interventions were evaluated both individually and in combination. However, the quality of the studies varied significantly, with many lacking critical methodological details necessary to assess the risk of bias. Only four studies were deemed to have a low risk of bias across all quality domains. When comparing long-term low-dose antibiotic prophylaxis to no treatment or placebo, the evidence suggested that antibiotics may make little or no difference in reducing the risk of repeat symptomatic UTIs (9 studies, 1667 children: risk ratio [RR] 0.77, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.54 to 1.09; low certainty evidence) or febrile UTIs (RR 0.83, 95% CI 0.56 to 1.21; low certainty evidence) over one to two years. Similarly, at one to three years, antibiotic prophylaxis appeared to have little or no effect on the risk of new or progressive renal damage as detected by DMSA scans (8 studies, 1503 children: RR 0.73, 95% CI 0.33 to 1.61; low certainty evidence). Adverse events were reported in four studies, with no significant differences between treatment groups (1056 children: RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.81 to 1.08). However, antibiotic use was associated with a threefold increase in the likelihood of bacterial drug resistance (187 UTIs: RR 2.97, 95% CI 1.54 to 5.74; moderate certainty evidence). Seven studies compared long-term antibiotic prophylaxis alone with surgical reimplantation of the ureters combined with antibiotics. Only two of these studies reported on febrile UTIs (429 children). The combination of surgery and antibiotics may reduce the risk of febrile UTIs by 57% (RR 0.43, 95% CI 0.27 to 0.70; moderate certainty evidence). However, there was little or no difference in the risk of new kidney defects detected by intravenous pyelogram at four to five years (4 studies, 572 children: RR 1.09, 95% CI 0.79 to 1.49; moderate certainty evidence). Four studies compared endoscopic injection treatments with antibiotics alone, with three reporting on febrile UTIs. The analysis showed little or no difference in the risk of febrile UTIs between the two approaches (RR 0.74, 95% CI 0.31 to 1.78; low certainty evidence). Additionally, four studies involving 425 children compared different materials used for endoscopic injection under the ureters, such as polydimethylsiloxane (Macroplastique), dextranomer/hyaluronic acid polymer (Deflux), glutaraldehyde cross-linked (GAX) collagen, and polyacrylate polyalcohol copolymer (VANTRIS). Only one study (255 children, low certainty evidence) reported on febrile UTIs, finding no difference between the materials. However, two studies comparing Macroplastique with Deflux suggested that Macroplastique may be superior in resolving VUR (3 months: RR 0.50, 95% CI 0.33 to 0.78; 12 months: RR 0.54, 95% CI 0.35 to 0.83; low certainty evidence). Two studies compared probiotics with antibiotics and found little or no difference in the risk of repeat symptomatic UTIs (RR 0.82, 95% CI 0.56 to 1.21; low certainty evidence). Single studies evaluated circumcision versus antibiotics, cranberry products versus no treatment, oxybutynin versus placebo, two different surgical techniques, and endoscopic injection versus no treatment, but the evidence from these studies was limited. In conclusion, compared to no treatment, long-term low-dose antibiotics may have little or no effect on reducing the number of repeat symptomatic or febrile UTIs in children with VUR (low certainty evidence). The variability in study designs and findings made it difficult to draw definitive conclusions about the efficacy of antibiotic treatment. The additional benefit of surgical or endoscopic correction of VUR over antibiotic treatment alone remains unclear due to the limited number of studies directly comparing these interventions and reporting relevant clinical outcomes.
